items.prompt: Identify which cost classification concerns whether total cost changes with output: total/average or fixed/variable.
items.canonical_answer: Fixed/variable (1).
marking_guidance: Characteristic: behaviour relative to output, 1.

items.prompt: Explain why fixed total cost and average fixed cost can move differently as output rises.
items.canonical_answer: The total commitment stays unchanged in the stated range (1), whereas dividing it over more units lowers the average per unit (1).
marking_guidance: Difference/distinguishing test: total versus per-unit amount, 1 each.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum
objective_titles: Define total, average, fixed and variable costs

items.prompt: Explain why N$2,000 premises cost spread across 500 items is N$4 per item but across 1,000 is N$2.
items.canonical_answer: The same total is divided by different output (1), so the per-unit fixed amount falls without the total commitment falling (1).
marking_guidance: Context: premises; reasoning: denominator grows 1; result: average not total falls 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum
objective_titles: Define total, average, fixed and variable costs

items.prompt: Explain what changes when receipts rise from N$4,000 on 200 sold units to N$5,400 on 300 sold units.
items.canonical_answer: Total revenue rises N$1,400, but average revenue falls from N$20 to N$18 per unit. More sales units outweigh the lower receipts per unit in the aggregate. These are revenue measures, not profit, because costs are absent.
marking_guidance: Relationship: total up/average down 1; evidence: N$20 to 18 and N$1,400 1; explanation: quantity offsets unit revenue and profit boundary 2.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why a seller receiving N$6,000 from sales with total cost N$4,800 should not call N$6,000 profit.
items.canonical_answer: N$6,000 is revenue before costs (1); profit is N$1,200 after subtracting the complete total cost (1).
marking_guidance: Context: stated receipts/cost; reasoning: cost deduction 1; result: N$1,200 profit 1.

items.prompt: Explain why average revenue is not the revenue earned from selling one extra unit.
items.canonical_answer: Average revenue is total revenue divided by all units sold, so it is revenue per unit sold (1); the revenue from one extra sale is marginal revenue, which can differ, for example when the price must be lowered to sell the extra unit (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: average revenue versus marginal revenue; boundary/test: revenue per unit sold versus revenue from one extra unit, 1 each.

items.prompt: Define the short run in production.
items.canonical_answer: The period in which at least one factor of production, such as premises, is fixed, so the firm has both fixed and variable costs.
marking_guidance: Meaning: at least one factor of production is fixed (1). Distinguishing feature: so costs divide into fixed and variable, unlike the long run when all can change (1).

items.prompt: Explain how more output can reduce average fixed cost without reducing total fixed cost.
items.canonical_answer: Initial change: output rises in the same capacity range (1); the firm spreads the unchanged commitment over more units, reducing its per-unit amount (1).
marking_guidance: Initial change 1; mechanism/effect for firm: fixed-cost spreading 1.

items.prompt: Explain why selling 600 units at N$9 gives less revenue than 500 at N$12.
items.canonical_answer: The new N$5,400 receipts are below the original N$6,000 (1), so the extra quantity does not offset the lower price in this comparison (1).
marking_guidance: Context: price/quantity pairs; reasoning: products calculated 1; result: revenue lower by N$600 1.

items.prompt: Define production technology.
items.canonical_answer: Methods and knowledge used to transform productive inputs into output.

items.prompt: Explain how suitable technology reducing material waste can affect production costs.
items.canonical_answer: Initial change: less input is wasted (1); the firm can make the same satisfactory output with fewer materials, potentially reducing relevant costs (1).
marking_guidance: Initial change 1; mechanism/effect for firm: less input per acceptable output lowers potential cost 1.

items.prompt: Explain why an equipment purchase alone does not establish a profitable production improvement.
items.canonical_answer: Operation, training and maintenance may add costs (1), while the output must meet quality and demand, so net financial benefit requires a complete comparison (1).

items.prompt: Define fixed cost.
items.canonical_answer: A cost that does not vary with output over the relevant period and capacity range; its level can change over time.

items.prompt: Define variable cost.

items.prompt: Calculate total revenue from 180 notebooks sold at N$25 each.
items.canonical_answer: Formula: price × quantity sold. Working: 25 × 180 = 4500. Answer: N$4,500.
marking_guidance: Formula/working for learning; answer unit N$4,500 earns the single result mark.

items.prompt: Explain why production of 200 notebooks and sales of 180 at N$25 give N$4,500 rather than N$5,000 revenue.
items.canonical_answer: Revenue uses sold units. The twenty unsold notebooks do not generate current sales receipts. Multiplying 180 by N$25 gives N$4,500; multiplying total production would count N$500 not received from sales.
marking_guidance: Relationship: sales versus output 1; evidence: 180/200 and N$500 difference 1; explanation: unsold units excluded 2.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why selling 220 units at N$20 can yield less revenue than selling 180 at N$25.
items.canonical_answer: The receipts are N$4,400 versus N$4,500 (1), so the lower price more than offsets the additional sold units here (1).
marking_guidance: Context: paired values; reasoning: correct products 1; result: N$100 fall despite more units 1.

items.prompt: Calculate average revenue from N$3,300 receipts on 150 units sold.
items.canonical_answer: Formula: total revenue/quantity sold. Working: 3300/150 = 22. Answer: N$22 per sold unit.
marking_guidance: Formula and working for learning; answer/unit N$22 per unit earns the single result mark.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why 100 units at N$24 and 50 at N$18 give average revenue N$22 rather than N$21.
items.canonical_answer: Receipts are N$3,300 across 150 units. The higher price applies to twice as many units, so total revenue divided by quantity is N$22. The simple unweighted mean N$21 ignores differing sales quantities.
marking_guidance: Relationship: quantity-weighted receipts 1; evidence: N$3,300/150 1; explanation: higher-price units have greater weight 2.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain when average revenue equals the stated selling price of identical units.
items.canonical_answer: If all units are sold at that one price (1), dividing price times quantity by the same sold quantity returns the price (1).
marking_guidance: Context: identical single-price sales; reasoning: same quantity denominator 1; result: price equality under condition 1.

items.prompt: The Ink Bay printer has monthly fixed cost N$2,000 and variable cost N$4 per booklet. Initially 500 booklets are produced and sold at N$12; later 1,000 are produced and sold at N$10. These are complete relevant costs for the illustration. (a) Describe three cost/revenue features (6). (b) Examine how expansion affects total and per-unit measures (7). (c) Suggest how the firm should use the comparison before choosing a continuing output plan (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Fixed cost stays N$2,000 within the range. Total variable cost rises N$2,000 to N$4,000. Price falls N$12 to N$10 while sold quantity doubles. (b) Total cost rises N$4,000 to N$6,000, while average cost falls N$8 to N$6. Revenue rises N$6,000 to N$10,000, and profit rises N$2,000 to N$4,000. Fixed-cost spreading helps explain lower average cost; the larger sales quantity offsets the lower price in these data. (c) The larger plan is more profitable among these stated monthly options. Before adopting it continuously, check that demand sustains 1,000 sales at N$10, quality remains suitable and the stated cost range continues. It is not evidence that further expansion gives the same result. The judgement depends on the specific complete costs and achieved sales rather than output alone.
marking_guidance: Context: Ink Bay. Parts/allocation: (a) fixed, variable, selling features 2 each = 6. (b) total/average cost 2, revenue/profit 3, mechanism 2 = 7. (c) supported current choice 2, relevant demand/capacity checks 3, conditional judgement 2 = 7.

items.prompt: (a) Define total cost (2). (b) Define average cost (2). (c) Explain why fixed does not mean unchanged forever (2). (d) Explain why constant variable cost per unit can coexist with rising total variable cost (2). (e) Explain why output alone does not determine revenue (2). (f) Explain when average revenue equals price (2). (g) Explain why revenue is not profit (2). (h) Explain one way technology can alter production requirements (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Fixed plus variable cost at stated output. (b) Total cost divided by output. (c) Fixed concerns output changes in a relevant period/range; terms or capacity can later change. (d) More units each using the same input amount raise the total. (e) Units must be sold at relevant prices. (f) All sold units use the same price, so dividing receipts by those units returns it. (g) Profit deducts total cost. (h) Less waste can reduce materials per satisfactory output, subject to suitability.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight 2-mark parts. (a) sum + output; (b) total/output + per-unit unit; (c) range + time change; (d) constant unit requirement + larger total; (e) sold quantity + price; (f) one price + ratio; (g) receipts + cost subtraction; (h) technology mechanism + output condition.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: The Seal Craft firm produces one product. It considers technology that reduces materials per item but adds an equipment commitment and training. Current sales are 300 units at N$20, and total current cost is N$4,500. The new plan predicts 400 sold units at N$18 but supplies no complete new cost total. (a) Define average revenue (2). (b) Explain current total revenue and profit (4). (c) Explain how the proposed technology could affect costs and revenue (7). (d) Discuss whether the new plan is proven more profitable (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Total revenue divided by quantity sold. (b) Revenue is N$6,000 and profit N$1,500 after total cost. (c) Lower materials use could reduce a variable requirement, but equipment and training add costs. New receipts would be N$7,200 if 400 sell at N$18. The lower average receipts are offset by more sales in the aggregate. Production capacity alone does not establish those sales. (d) Higher projected receipts are a potential advantage, but complete new cost and demand evidence are absent. The difference in receipts cannot be labelled a profit increase. Seek equipment, operation and training costs plus credible sales evidence before choosing. The new plan is more profitable only if complete costs relative to achieved revenue support it; the current information does not prove that.
marking_guidance: Context: Seal Craft. Parts/allocation: (a) receipts/quantity 1, per-unit qualifier 1. (b) revenue calculation/meaning 2, profit calculation/deduction 2 = 4. (c) variable requirement 2, new commitments 2, receipts and sales condition 3 = 7. (d) revenue case 2, omitted cost/demand limit 2, conditional judgement 3 = 7. Mechanism: material saving competes with new equipment commitments and uncertain sales.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a workshop should regard a falling average cost as sufficient evidence that expanding production improves profit when sales quantity and price effects are unknown (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: lower cost per satisfactory unit can improve the scope for a profit margin and may reflect fixed-cost spreading or productive improvement. Against: total cost may rise, extra output may remain unsold and a lower selling price may be needed. Average cost alone does not describe receipts or the full aggregate difference. Judgement: compare total revenue and complete total cost for feasible sold quantities and the relevant period. The condition for a profit improvement is a larger net difference after those changes; lower average cost alone does not establish it.
marking_guidance: Argument for: cost-per-unit potential developed, up to 4. Argument against: total cost/sales/price limits developed, up to 4. Judgement: distinct complete net-result condition, 1. Total 9.

items.prompt: Define total revenue.
items.canonical_answer: The amount received from sales; for a single product at one price, price multiplied by quantity sold.
marking_guidance: Meaning: total sales receipts (1); distinguishing feature: price multiplied by quantity sold when all units sell at one price (1). Unsold output and loans are not sales receipts.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring; approved 6145 revision-01 nonvisual scope

items.prompt: Define average revenue.
items.canonical_answer: Total revenue divided by quantity sold, which is the revenue received per unit sold (1); when every unit sells at the same price, average revenue equals that price (1).
marking_guidance: Meaning: total revenue divided by quantity sold, that is, revenue per unit sold (1); distinguishing feature: equals the selling price when all units sell at one price (1). Do not credit the extra revenue from one additional sale.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring; approved 6145 revision-01 nonvisual scope
